title: US Moves to Strip Work Permits From H-1B Spouses, Threatening Indian Families
excerpt: The Trump administration has added a proposed rule to end H-4 EAD employment authorization, a program that nearly 100,000 Indian spouses depend on during decade-long green card waits.
body:
• The Trump administration has added a proposed rule to DHS's regulatory agenda that would eliminate employment authorization for H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B workers, reversing a 2015 Obama-era policy.
  • Nearly 100,000 Indian spouses are estimated to hold H-4 EADs, and over one million Indians — including dependents — are stuck in the employment-based green card backlog.
  • The proposal is classified as a "Long-Term Action" with no draft text or timeline, meaning no immediate change for current H-4 EAD holders.
  • The move comes alongside other H-1B restrictions, including a proposed $103,265 fee for new hires and the elimination of the 60-day grace period after job loss.

The Trump administration is moving to end work permits for spouses of H-1B visa holders, a step that could strip employment authorization from nearly 100,000 Indian spouses and upend the financial stability of families already facing decades-long green card waits.

A notice titled "Removing H-4 Dependent Spouses From the Classes of Noncitizens Eligible for Employment Authorization" has appeared on the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs website under the Department of Homeland Security's long-term regulatory agenda, according to Bloomberg Law. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has completed a proposed regulation to eliminate the program and sent it to the White House Office of Management and Budget for review.

What the H-4 EAD Program Provides

The H-4 Employment Authorization Document program was created in 2015 under the Obama administration. It allows certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B workers to apply for work authorization — but only if the H-1B holder has an approved I-140 immigrant petition or has been granted H-1B status beyond the standard six-year limit while pursuing a green card.

In practice, this means the H-4 EAD is available almost exclusively to families deep in the green card process — people who have already been approved for permanent residence but are waiting for a visa number. For Indian nationals, that wait can stretch 10 to 20 years or more due to per-country caps.

The work permit serves a dual purpose: it provides a second household income during what can be a decade-plus wait, and it allows spouses — the majority of whom are women with professional qualifications — to maintain careers and professional relevance in the U.S. workforce.

Who Would Be Affected

Indians account for the overwhelming majority of H-4 EAD holders. A recent analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy estimated that more than one million Indians, including dependents, were waiting in the first three employment-based green card categories as of December 2025. Many of these families depend on the H-4 spouse's earnings.

"If the programme were eventually abolished, these families could face a major disruption to their lives."

— LiveMint

The financial impact would vary by household, but for families in high-cost areas like the Bay Area, Seattle, or New Jersey — where a large share of H-1B workers are concentrated — losing a second income during a multi-year green card wait could force difficult decisions about staying in the United States.

No Immediate Change — But Part of a Pattern

Immigration attorneys stress that no change has taken effect. The item is classified as a "Long-Term Action" with no draft text available and no deadline set for a formal proposed rule. Before the H-4 EAD program could be eliminated, DHS would need to publish a proposed rule, invite public comments, respond to those comments, issue a final rule, and set an effective date. That process typically takes months.

But the proposal does not exist in isolation. It is the latest in a series of measures restricting H-1B employment. In the past week alone, DHS proposed a new $103,265 fee for new H-1B hires and the White House cleared a separate proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period that allows workers to find new sponsorship after losing a job.

Bloomberg Law reports that the administration first announced its intent to end H-4 work permits in early 2017 during Trump's first term but never finalized a rule. A long-running legal battle over the program's legality ended last year when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge, after the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals found Congress had granted the executive branch authority to extend work authorization to H-4 spouses.

What It Means for Indian Families

For Indian H-1B families, the proposal represents the convergence of several pressures. The per-country green card backlog means Indian applicants wait far longer than nationals from any other country. During that wait, the H-4 EAD has allowed spouses to build careers, contribute to household income, and maintain financial security in a country where they cannot adjust their status.

Business groups have argued that removing work eligibility for H-1B spouses would harm recruitment and retention of foreign talent, making it harder for companies to attract skilled workers who know their families will face indefinite work restrictions.

Immigration attorney Rajiv Khanna told NDTV that existing work authorizations are not at immediate risk, but cautioned that the policy direction is clear. Families currently holding H-4 EADs should continue to file renewals on time and consult with immigration counsel about their options.

What to Watch

The timeline for a formal proposed rule remains undefined. The public comment period, once opened, will be a critical window for advocacy organizations, business groups, and affected families to register opposition. Congressional action — either through standalone legislation or as part of broader immigration reform — remains another potential avenue, though the prospects for legislative relief in the current political environment are uncertain.
nri_angle: Nearly 100,000 Indian spouses hold H-4 EADs, and eliminating the program would directly impact Indian families facing the longest green card backlogs of any nationality.
